title: Christmas Pageant Platform
subject: Torts
subtopic: Standard of Due Care / Contributory Negligence / Causation
stem:
Original row used: BARMATRIX Q# 20649, Torts, official key A. The source row asks which added fact would most likely produce judgment for an independent contractor in an all-or-nothing contributory-negligence jurisdiction.

Chosen variation title: The Christmas Pageant Platform

Naomi worked for Lydia’s private pageant-production company, which was staging a Christian Christmas pageant. The company hired Barnabas, an independent contractor, to adjust the idle setting on a motorized rolling platform that carried a large manger prop. Barnabas adjusted the idle setting too high. Later, Naomi stood beside the platform and pressed the start switch to move it; because the platform lacked a roll-stop interlock, it lurched and injured her.

Naomi asserted a negligence claim against Barnabas. Which one of the following additional facts or inferences, if it were the only one true, would be most likely to result in a judgment for Barnabas in a jurisdiction that applies the all-or-nothing rule of contributory negligence?
call: Which one of the following additional facts or inferences, if it were the only one true, would be most likely to result in a judgment for Barnabas in a jurisdiction that applies the all-or-nothing rule of contributory negligence?

choices.A: The company that previously rented the platform failed to notify Lydia's company that the platform needed a roll-stop interlock.
choices.B: If Naomi had been standing on the operator step when she started the platform, she would not have been injured.
choices.C: Rolling pageant platforms of this type are usually equipped with roll-stop interlocks.
choices.D: The absence of a roll-stop interlock was a manufacturing defect in the platform.

rightExplanation:
C is correct. The call asks for the added fact most likely to produce judgment for Barnabas. If platforms of this type usually have roll-stop interlocks, then Barnabas may reasonably have expected the interlock to prevent the platform from lurching even after an idle adjustment. That fact attacks Barnabas’s own negligence: it weakens foreseeability of the risk created by the idle adjustment.

Gold Key: Negligence turns on unreasonable conduct in light of foreseeable risk. A fact that makes the particular risk not foreseeable can defeat breach.

Silver Key: In a “which added fact helps the defendant win” array, prefer the fact that breaks an element of the plaintiff’s claim over facts that merely blame someone else or describe a safer hypothetical.

c3.label: CUT A
c3.text: wrong-party / other-actor bait. It answers “who else failed?” not “what fact defeats Barnabas’s negligence.”

c3.label: CUT B
c3.text: wrong-element contributory-negligence bait. It proves avoidability, not Naomi’s negligence.

c3.label: CUT D
c3.text: wrong-frame / other-cause bait. It identifies a product-defect cause, not a contractor-liability defense.

c3.label: Residual
c3.text: C. It is the only fact that attacks Barnabas’s own breach by making the lurching risk less foreseeable.

c3.label: CLASH
c3.text: If B and C survive, the axis is “plaintiff fault vs defendant no-breach.” The splitting fact is that B never says Naomi acted negligently, while C speaks directly to foreseeability of Barnabas’s risk.

studentScript: Call: which added fact helps Barnabas win. Cut other-party blame and other-cause blame. Cut the plaintiff-position answer because it shows avoidability, not negligence. Pick C because usual interlocks make the lurching risk less foreseeable.

A.signal: The choice blames the previous rental company, but the call asks what helps Barnabas win Naomi's negligence claim against him.
A.lawyer: A third party's failure to warn Lydia's company does not itself defeat Barnabas's liability if Barnabas's own negligent adjustment foreseeably caused the injury.

B.signal: The choice says Naomi would have avoided injury in another position. It does not say her actual position was careless.
B.lawyer: Contributory negligence requires negligent plaintiff conduct contributing to the accident. Mere but-for avoidability does not establish that element.

C.signal: This choice is the only one aimed at Barnabas's own negligence. It says the missing safety feature is usually present.
C.lawyer: If platforms of this type usually have roll-stop interlocks, Barnabas may not reasonably foresee that the idle adjustment would cause the platform to lurch; that can defeat breach.

D.signal: The choice identifies a defect in the platform, not a reason Barnabas's own adjustment was non-negligent.
D.lawyer: A manufacturing defect may make a manufacturer liable, but another contributing cause does not automatically relieve a negligent contractor.

goldKeys.statement: Negligence turns on unreasonable conduct in light of a foreseeable risk. A fact that makes the specific risk not foreseeable can defeat breach.
goldKeys.trigger: The added fact says the missing safety device is usually present.
goldKeys.unlocks: Why the normal presence of a roll-stop interlock helps the contractor.
goldKeys.authority: Restatement (Third) of Torts: Liability for Physical and Emotional Harm § 3; negligence factors include foreseeable likelihood/severity and burden of precautions.

goldKeys.statement: Contributory negligence requires negligent plaintiff conduct that contributed to the harm. A fact that the plaintiff would have avoided injury by doing something else is not enough by itself.
goldKeys.trigger: The answer says the plaintiff would not have been hurt from another position.
goldKeys.unlocks: Why the plaintiff-position answer is a trap.
goldKeys.authority: Common-law contributory negligence rule; see Cornell Wex summary.

silverKeys.statement: In an added-fact defense question, sort each option by what it attacks: defendant breach, plaintiff negligence, other cause, or other party. The best defense fact usually attacks an element of the plaintiff's claim against this defendant.
silverKeys.trigger: Choices point in four different blame directions.

remediation.title: Avoidability is not contributory negligence
remediation.signal: Choice says plaintiff would have avoided injury if she had acted differently.
remediation.studentMove: Ask whether the choice says the actual conduct was negligent.
remediation.tinyRule: No plaintiff negligence, no contributory-negligence bar.
remediation.trap: Confusing safer hypothetical with legal fault.
